risk_rationale: Inflation remains materially above target — CPI at 3.8% and Core PCE at 3.2% — while oil's $3.98 single-session drop signals demand fragility or supply shock dynamics that complicate the Fed's path. Labor market deceleration (115K NFP, wage growth slipping to 3.6%) alongside a 3.6% savings rate leaves the consumer with limited buffer against further shocks.
outlook_headline: Stagflationary crosscurrents intensify: sticky inflation, softening labor, and an oil shock in motion.
outlook_body: The macro backdrop is deteriorating at the margin — real GDP at 2.0% annualized is holding, but the composition of risk is worsening. Headline CPI at 3.8% and Core PCE at 3.2% keep the Fed pinned even as the labor market loses momentum, a classic late-cycle trap. The sharp WTI drop to $105.78 introduces a bifurcated risk: if demand-driven, it signals growth deterioration; if supply-driven, it provides temporary inflation relief but masks underlying fragility. With the savings rate at 3.6% and credit card delinquencies at 2.9%, the consumer is running out of shock absorbers.

tabs.gdp: Real GDP growth of 2.0% annualized is holding above stall speed but the underlying composition is increasingly fragile against the backdrop of an oil shock and tightening consumer balance sheets. The combination of slowing NFP, a 3.6% savings rate, and WTI at $109.8 creates a credible path to sub-1% growth within two quarters. Inventory and net export dynamics could provide temporary offsets, but domestic demand is the linchpin and it is weakening.
tabs.jobs: NFP at 115K is a meaningful step down and sits below the ~150K threshold generally associated with labor market stability at current participation levels. U-3 at 4.3% and U-6 at 8.2% — a 390bp gap — indicates elevated underemployment and part-time slack that the headline rate is masking. The labor market is a lagging indicator; at this pace of deceleration, unemployment is likely to drift higher into Q3 2026.
tabs.unemp: U-3 at 4.3% represents a meaningful rise from cycle lows and confirms the labor market is no longer a source of macro resilience. The U-6 underemployment rate at 8.2% — a 190bp spread over U-3 — signals significant slack in hours and involuntary part-time work that the headline number obscures. This breadth of labor market weakness is inconsistent with a soft-landing narrative and points to genuine demand destruction in the jobs market.
tabs.wages: Wage growth decelerated 30bp to 3.6% YoY, narrowing the gap with CPI at 3.8% and leaving real wages negative on a headline basis. This is a dual negative: it reduces consumer purchasing power at a time when the savings rate is already thin at 3.6%, and it signals that labor market tightness is easing faster than the Fed may have anticipated. From an inflation standpoint, moderating wages reduce services inflation pressure, but the relief is insufficient given Core PCE still running at 3.2%.
tabs.cpi: Headline CPI at 3.8% YoY is running nearly 90bp above Core CPI at 2.7%, a gap almost entirely attributable to energy — WTI at $109.8 is the dominant driver and it is not yet fully reflected in downstream prices. Core CPI at 2.7% has not broken to target and risks re-acceleration as oil costs transmit through transportation, manufacturing, and services over the next 60-90 days. The Fed cannot cut rates with headline at 3.8% and an oil shock still propagating; rate relief is not imminent.
tabs.pce: Core PCE at 3.2% — the Fed's preferred measure — remains 120bp above target and is the single most important number blocking any dovish pivot. Headline PCE at 3.5% reflects the same energy-driven wedge seen in CPI, and the savings rate at 3.6% confirms consumers are drawing down buffers rather than reducing spending voluntarily. The combination of elevated PCE, depleted savings, and surging energy costs represents a serious deterioration in the consumer's real income trajectory.
tabs.yield: The 10Y-2Y spread has re-steepened to 48bp, suggesting markets are beginning to price in eventual Fed easing, but the 10Y at 4.46% reflects persistent inflation risk premium. With Fed Funds at 3.64% and Core PCE at 3.2%, real policy rates are modestly positive but insufficient to declare victory on inflation. The Fed remains effectively on hold — cutting risks re-igniting inflation, while holding risks accelerating labor market deterioration.
tabs.credit: IG OAS at 78bp remains historically tight and reflects a market that has not yet priced the deteriorating macro backdrop — this is a complacency risk, not a green light. HY OAS at 279bp is wider but still well below levels consistent with recession conditions (typically 500bp+), suggesting high yield is also mispriced relative to the unemployment and growth trajectory. A repricing of credit risk, particularly in energy-cost-sensitive sectors and highly leveraged consumer-facing businesses, remains the key tail risk.
tabs.housing: The 30-year mortgage at 6.37% continues to lock existing homeowners in place and suppress transaction volume, while Housing Starts at 1,502K suggest builders are still active but are running ahead of effective demand at current affordability levels. With real wages flat, savings rates thin, and no near-term prospect of meaningful mortgage rate relief, the demand side of housing remains structurally impaired. A downside break in starts and permits over coming months would be a significant recessionary signal.
tabs.oil: WTI dropped $3.98 to $105.78 and Brent sits at $111.4 — the magnitude of the single-session move warrants immediate attention as to whether this is demand destruction signaling or a supply-side release. At $105+ WTI, energy remains a persistent inflation input that prevents the Fed from pivoting, and the Brent-WTI spread of $5.62 suggests ongoing geopolitical or logistics premium in global crude. A sustained move lower in WTI would provide headline CPI relief, but if driven by demand collapse, the macro trade-off is unfavorable.
tabs.banks: Credit card delinquency at 2.9% is a direct stress indicator for consumer lending books and is trending in the wrong direction given the 4.3% unemployment rate and near-zero real wage growth. Net interest income should remain supported by the 10Y-2Y spread at 47bp, but rising loss provisions for consumer credit will increasingly offset NII tailwinds in bank earnings. Banks with high consumer credit card and auto loan exposure face a deteriorating credit quality outlook that the current spread environment is not compensating for.

signal_flags.note: A $3.98 single-session drop at elevated absolute levels requires immediate classification — demand destruction would confirm growth deterioration; supply release would offer temporary inflation relief but does not resolve underlying macro stress.

Wage deceleration below headline CPI (3.8%) turns real wages negative, compressing consumer spending capacity at a time when the savings rate (3.6%) provides minimal cushion. Continued deceleration would accelerate labor market deterioration feedback loop.
Core PCE at 3.2% is 120bp above the Fed's 2% target and prevents any near-term dovish pivot; combined with softening labor data, this locks the Fed into an increasingly uncomfortable hold posture.
Below-trend job creation at 115K, if sustained, will push U-3 unemployment higher in coming months — a lagging confirmation of the slowdown already visible in leading indicators.
At 3.6%, the personal savings rate leaves households with minimal buffer against income shocks or further credit tightening; elevated CC delinquencies at 2.9% reinforce consumer stress at the margin.
